blocks.text: Therefore, since it is not possible to inquire more precisely into the kinds of locusts, how much better it is here to confess our ignorance frankly than to be carried off the path with a very famous translator, who rendered the words of the Law thus, Levit. XI, 20. 21. 22. Every flying creeping thing that goes on four feet shall be an abomination to you. Yet this you shall eat of every flying creeping thing that goes on four feet: that which does not have legs above its feet with which to leap upon the earth. Of these you shall eat these: the locust after its kind, and the silkworm after its kind, and the beetle after its kind, and the cicada after its kind. In this version there are many errors. First, in verse twenty-one, it changes an affirmative into a negative, against the most evident meaning of the Law. For in verse twenty the eating of every insect that flies and goes on four feet is forbidden. But in verse twenty-one an exception is made for flying insects which, besides four feet, have two leaping legs, such as the four kinds of locust named in verse twenty-two. Yet the translator proceeds as if, of the creeping things, or flying four-footed insects, the Law permitted only those that do not have those leaping legs. On that assumption, why does he at once add, you shall eat the locust, which everyone knows has those larger legs? Moreover, why are the bombyx [silkworm] and the cantharus [beetle], or scarabaeus [scarab], placed in this list? The former does not fly as long as it remains a silkworm; and neither is four-footed, neither [col. 452] has been used as food by any nation, much less by the Jews, whose cleanliness in eating was of the highest. We know that in Ethiopia and elsewhere there were ἀκριδοφάγους [akridophagous] and ὀφιοφάγους [ophiophagous]; [III, 268] but there is no one who has mentioned τῶν βομβυκοφάγων [tōn bombykophagōn] or τῶν κανθαροφάγων [tōn kantharophagōn]. Human nature has always shrunk from such foul and fetid foods. So that most learned man ought not to have set them on Jewish tables, and that as though on God's authority. I will say, however, why he rendered these words, אשר לו כרעים ממעל לרגליו, which has legs above its feet, with an added negation, which does not have, etc. It is well known that certain words of the Prophets are read otherwise than they are written. Among these is the little word לו, which the Masoretes note is written לא in fifteen places and read לו; of which the former means not, the latter to it. So in this place, while the text writes אשר לא כרעים, which has not legs, the margin has אשר לו כרעים, which has legs. It is certain that this reading must be followed, both from the whole sequence of the text and from the agreement of the translators. For all the Hebrews read thus. Nor do the Greeks, Jerome, the two Chaldees (Jonathan and Onkelos), the Syriac, the four Arabic translators (whom I was able to consult, two printed, and two in manuscript in Sweden), the Samaritan, etc., follow anything else, not to mention that the Hebrew copy of the Samaritans has in the text itself לו with Vav, not with Aleph ^{(22)}.

Moses describes the clean locusts as flying and four-footed. Flying, to set them against the ἀπτέροις [apterois], such as the attelabi in Pliny and the asiracus in Dioscorides ^{(23)}. The Talmudists assign them four wings. Hence it is that in Greek they are called τετραπτερυλλίδες [tetrapterullides], that is, four-winged. Aristophanes in the Acharnians:
Ἀλλ᾽ εἴ τι βούλει πρίασο τῶν ἐγὼ φέρω, Τῶν ὀρταλίχων, ἢ τῶν τετραπτερυλλίδων· [All᾽ ei ti boulei priaso tōn egō pherō, Tōn ortalichōn, ē tōn tetrapterullidōn]
